rule: Stop the scroll in the first 1 to 2 seconds with motion, and state the value, the offer, the price or the result within 3 seconds. The first frame must make sense with no sound.
short: Motion in the first frame; the value, offer, price or result within 3 s; it must read with no sound.
why: Top ads keep 50 to 60% of viewers at 3 s; most people watch muted. 11 of 17 Rwandan ads put the price, offer or number up in the first 3 s.

rule: Put the price (or the offer in a few words) in the first frame, large, in the top third of the screen, not in a bottom caption.
short: The price (or the offer) in the first frame, large, top third.
why: The long-running East African Facebook ads all show the offer at second 0 (48,000RWF, PROMO FOR 5K, Offer today at Kes 2,100).

rule: Put a large first caption of about 5 words on screen at 0.0 s, in the upper-middle.
short: A first caption of about 5 words at 0.0 s, upper-middle.
why: 63% of top ads use text in the first frame (source claim); the platform UI covers the bottom.

rule: Write the hook in plain person-style words: a question, a POV line or 'I found ...', not a brand slogan.
short: Hook in plain person words (a question, 'POV: ...', 'I found ...'), not a slogan.
why: The repeated hooks were 'Urgent order?', 'POV: You just found ...', 'Nobody warns you ...'.

rule: Show the product doing its job (or the result) before any persuasion: in the first 3 s, and at least 3 uses, angles or colours within 10 s.
short: Show it working (or the result) in the first 3 s, and 3 uses, angles or colours within 10 s.
why: The blender doing juice, mango and grains answers 'what can I use it for'; a steamer demo with no text got 235.8K likes.

rule: In a before/after, show the result first ('After' or 'Wait for it...'), then the before, then the process, then the offer.
why: Several of the before/after clips open on the after frame; the reward up front keeps people watching.

rule: Default 15 to 25 s for products and offers; 6 to 9 s for a one-idea clip; a 5 s loop is enough for gifts and fashion; 30 to 60 s only with a talking host (clinic, property, restaurant tour). Never over 30 s without a reason.
short: 15 to 25 s for products and offers, 6 to 9 s for one idea, a 5 s loop for gifts and fashion.
why: Rwandan Facebook video ads run a median 34 s, about half under 30 s (under 20 s for products and offers, 40 to 90 s with a talking person); top-CTR TikTok ads cluster at 15 to 25 s.

rule: Change the shot or the text every 2 to 4 seconds (about 3 to 5 changes per 10 s); kinetic text and colour-beat ads can go to 8 to 10.
short: A new shot or text change every 2 to 4 s.
why: Product, price and phone clips ran 3 to 5 cuts per 10 s; the fastest motion-graphics ads change colour about once a second.

rule: One product, one idea, one offer per video.
why: One product, one price, one number (Best Burgers) runs; mixed messages lose muted viewers.

rule: Put proof in the middle: a real customer reacting, the product working, a real shop full of stock, a real number from the owner.
why: Real customers eating or trying the product drove local engagement more than polish.

rule: For a 3D look, float the product in the middle with 4 to 8 ingredients, splashes or bubbles around it; one colour or a simple set behind, shallow depth of field.
why: The best 3D ads suspend the product with what it is made of around it (serum in bubbles, bread slices, milk-tea splashes).

rule: Use a three-beat reveal: 0-2 s a macro detail with a rim light; then the full product in a themed set with a slow orbit or push-in; the last 2-3 s the brand or price card on a clean background.
why: A 17 s and a 24 s premium example both follow it and end on the brand name in wide-spaced capitals.

rule: Make giant text part of the scene: the product name or the flavour or colour word, huge, behind or beside the product, cut by the frame edge, swapping colour per beat.
why: BREAD, BLURE and FRUIT / MILKTEA all do it; it reads at a glance and looks designed.

rule: Animate text on the beat: one phrase of 2 to 4 words per beat with one highlighted key word, pop-in with overshoot or a slide with motion blur, each held 0.5 to 1.5 s. A locked camera for text cards, a moving camera for products.
short: One phrase of 2 to 4 words per beat, one key word highlighted, each held 0.5 to 1.5 s.
why: Every kinetic typography example uses one phrase at a time with one key word in colour.

rule: Keep the phone or WhatsApp number on screen from second 0 to the last frame, in a fixed bar (top, or a lower-middle band above the app's UI), big digits grouped the way people read them.
short: The phone/WhatsApp number on screen from 0 s to the last frame, in a fixed bar above the app's UI, digits grouped.
why: A permanent phone bar is the commonest pattern in Rwandan ads (Eguriro, EHA 250, Kex Group, homeofhybrid, Elohome); only brands with budgets skip the number, small sellers never do.

rule: Show the price as a solid box that stays up, or as a label riding on each product shot; a price list is one card that stays long enough to read.
short: The price in a solid box that stays up, or a label riding on each product.
why: Price cards are solid boxes in the Rwandan sample; East African sellers label every product (150/=, KSH 35).

rule: Place the price, the claim and the call to action in the top third or the middle; never in the bottom 15%, which the app's username and caption cover.
short: Price, claim and call to action in the top third or middle, never the bottom 15% (the app covers it).
why: On 9:16 the platform UI covers the bottom; Facebook winners put price and number in the top third.

rule: Never more than 2 lines of text at once: short sticker words that change with the beat for the story, and a fixed strip for the price and the phone.
short: At most 2 lines of text at once: short beat words plus a fixed price/phone strip.
why: homeofhybrid spells a sentence with one word sticker per beat over a permanent phone bar (468 days running).

rule: Animate spec words in as they are said: one phrase at a time, white bold with an outline or in white rounded boxes.
why: Phone shops in Kigali do exactly this ('One SIM + eSIM', 'Accessories included').

rule: Always burn in captions, even when someone speaks: sentence by sentence in a box, or word by word.
short: Burn in captions for every spoken line (most people watch muted).
why: Most viewers watch muted; the clinic's boxed captions match the speech so the 60 s talk still works.

rule: The Seedance clip has no text: open on motion, keep the top third and a lower-middle band visually calm for the price strip and the phone bar BuPulse adds on top, and end on a clean hero shot with space above it.
short: No text in the clip: open on motion, keep the top third and a lower-middle band calm for BuPulse's price strip and phone bar, end on a clean hero shot with space above.
why: Seedance garbles letters; the winning ads still need the price and the number on screen from second 0, so they are added as an overlay.

rule: End with ONE named way to order, in the middle of the frame: 'WhatsApp {phone}', 'Call {phone}', 'Order on {app}', 'Find us at {landmark}' or 'DM now before stock ends' (only if stock is really limited).
short: End with ONE named way to order in the middle of the frame (WhatsApp, call, the app, the landmark).
why: Of 51 Rwandan Facebook video ads, 22 use the WhatsApp button, 13 send to Instagram and 4 to 'Call now'; 35 put the number in the caption.

rule: Put the offer and the price as a large overlay and repeat them in the call to action.
why: The viewer who decides at the end sees the reason and the route together.

rule: Add one trust line when the owner gives it: 'Pay after delivery', 'Free delivery in Kigali', 'Free delivery from 50k', '30 days return', a real address.
short: One trust line only if the owner gave it: pay after delivery, free delivery, returns, the address.
why: 'Free delivery' plus 'Pay after delivery' is the loudest pattern of the cash-on-delivery sellers that ran 7 to 24 months.

rule: Name the area and a landmark the way Kigali people give directions (Gishushu, Kicukiro Sonatube, UTC, T2000 House Room 213B), on the end card or in the caption.
why: Of 51 Rwandan Facebook ads, the addresses are landmarks, not streets ('Next to DELIGHT HOTEL', 'opposite IPRC traffic lights', 'same building as boho, door 8'): this is how Kigali people find places.

rule: Run a recurring offer as a weekly series with the same badge and layout (Tuesday pizza, Wednesday burger, lunch Monday to Friday).
why: Kigali restaurants already do it; a series builds the habit and is cheap to repeat.

rule: A percentage off always comes with the real price ('37.5% off: 5K'); a was/now anchor only when the owner gives both prices.
why: Pairing the percentage with a concrete price makes the saving feel real.

rule: If there is a voice-over, it starts by 0.5 s; music stays under the voice; one sound effect on each reveal.
why: Voice-over by 0.5 s and a first cut by 1.5 s is the pacing of top ads (secondary sources).

rule: The voice cannot speak Kinyarwanda or Swahili: for those businesses the on-screen text and the caption stay in the content language and the voice speaks English (Claude engine); the Seedance clip has music and ambient sound only.
short: The voice cannot speak Kinyarwanda or Swahili: say lines in English, on-screen text and caption in the content language (Seedance: music and ambience only).
why: Owner rule, 17 October 2026 (voice-language.ts).

rule: Match the audience: in Rwanda, English for products and prices and Kinyarwanda for the hook and the invitation; Swahili in Tanzania; English in Kenya and Uganda. Write numbers and money the local way (38,000 RWF, 48K, 400K / month).
short: Rwanda: English for products and prices, Kinyarwanda for the hook and the invitation; money the local way (38,000 RWF, 48K).
why: 13 of 51 Rwandan ads have Kinyarwanda captions (property and cheap goods lean Kinyarwanda; hotels, clinics, tech and beauty lean English); Cleopatra Home writes the caption twice, English then Kinyarwanda.

rule: When a host appears, let them open with a Kinyarwanda greeting on screen ('Muraho', 'Murakaza neza').
why: A local welcome plus a real shop floor builds trust (Abby Home).

rule: Show a real place behind the product (the shop shelf, the counter, the table, the compound) and a real person or real hands; not a blank studio.
short: A real place behind the product (shelf, counter, table, compound) and real people or hands; no blank studio.
why: Real shops with real people got more local engagement than premium AI clips; real cars in a real compound ran 15 months.

rule: If there is no presenter, use hands on the product (lifting, unwrapping, turning, pouring).
why: Hands unwrapping a burger or holding phones carry the long-running local ads.

rule: Default to a native, phone-made look for local sellers; keep the premium 3D and cinematic looks for premium products, and even then keep the price and the number in the motion.
short: A native phone-made look for local sellers; premium 3D only for premium products, still with price and number.
why: AI cinematic product clips had 3K to 7K likes; a phone shop's counter clip had 67.8K.

rule: Write the post caption with: the price in RWF, the area and a landmark, the delivery promise only if true, the phone number twice, and 3 to 4 hashtags with the city.
short: Caption: price in RWF, area and landmark, delivery only if true, the number twice, 3 to 4 city hashtags.
why: 35 of 51 Rwandan ads put the number in the caption; the caption carries the spec list (price, size, area, water and power, title, delivery): the video is the proof, the caption is the contract.

rule: Use local hashtags first (#kigalitiktok, #rwandatiktok, #KigaliRwanda, #KigaliBusiness) plus one broad tag (#fyp).
why: All the Rwandan sellers in the sample tag the city and the country.

rule: Make 3 to 5 variants of every product (price hook, pain hook, POV hook, demo only, offer only); keep the best running and add to it instead of replacing it.
short: Versions differ by hook: price, pain, POV, demo only, offer only.
why: Rwandan ads are young (most started in the last two weeks), so the number of variants live at once is the better signal: Derma 15, Elohome 8, Magic Chef 7, Piramie 6 in 11 days.

rule: Make a series, not one-offs ('New stock Sunday', 'Shop finds Ep 2', one dish per video), with the same layout each time.
why: Numbered series and one-dish-per-video advertisers keep viewers coming back.

rule: When the owner accepts MoMo, say it ('Pay with MoMo') in the end card and the caption.
why: None of the 51 Rwandan Facebook video ads mentions MoMo, M-Pesa or Airtel Money: an easy way to stand out.

rule: Make the 9:16 clip so it works on TikTok and as a Facebook ad (price and number in the picture, not only in the caption); change the caption per platform.
why: Facebook advertisers reuse their TikTok clips (TikTok watermarks visible in at least 3 ads).

rule: One idea and one price (or one offer) on screen from frame 0 and pinned there: a price pill at the top or a bar in the lower third, the same on every frame.
short: One price or offer pinned from frame 0 (a top pill or a lower-third bar), the same on every frame.
why: The most repeated Rwandan ads all do it: '20 Mbps | 20K / month' (Piramie, 6 variants in 11 days), '48,000RWF', 'Price: 500k', '350M RWF', 'Price: 16M'.

rule: Never show income proof or payment screenshots: no fake M-Money or bank SMS ('You have received 85000 RWF'), no piles of cash, no 'get rich' lines.
short: No income proof: no fake M-Money or bank SMS, no cash piles, no 'get rich' lines.
why: Seen in AI-labelled clips from a WhatsApp seller; a questionable claim format that destroys trust and breaks ad policy.

rule: Never invent a price, a discount, a stock count ('only a few left'), an end date, a delivery promise, an award, a result or a number.
short: No invented price, discount, stock count, end date, delivery promise, award or result.
why: Owner rule for every engine; the ad must be true for the business that posts it.

rule: No 'best', 'cheapest', 'biggest' or 'most affordable in Kigali' unless the owner wrote it; then use their words exactly.
short: No 'best', 'cheapest', 'most affordable in Kigali' unless the owner wrote it.
why: Superlatives are common in the research (BEST BURGERS IN KIGALI, THE MOST CHEAPEST IPHONES) but only the business can stand behind them.

rule: No skin, body, weight or medical before/after and no health promises (tummy trimming, curing snoring, clearing acne).
short: No skin, body, weight or medical before/after, no health promises.
why: Seen in the research (split-face breakouts, body massager claims) but against Meta and TikTok policy and the owner's rules.

rule: No fake reviews, testimonials or comments: a fictional presenter never claims to be a real customer, and a 'Replying to' card only quotes a real question.
short: No fake reviews or comments; a fictional presenter never poses as a real customer.
why: UGC and comment-reply formats work because viewers believe them.

rule: No famous brands, logos or people that are not the business's own, and no lookalikes (the AI 'McDonald's' or 'Dior' style ads are not to be copied).
short: No famous brands, logos, people or lookalikes that are not the business's own.
why: Trademark and likeness rules; AI-creator showcase clips use them, client ads must not.

rule: Never leave another app's watermark or template tag in the video (TikTok logo, CapCut tag).
short: No other app's watermark or template tag.
why: Facebook ads that reuse TikTok clips show the TikTok watermark; it looks second-hand.

rule: Do not copy the AI-creator wrapper (the prompt first, 'How to make this', 'Comment PROMPT') into a client's ad.
short: No 'how I made this' / 'Comment PROMPT' wrapper in a client ad.
why: It sells the tool, not the product; it is engagement bait for creators.

rule: No vague or choose-your-own discounts ('Drop 40% or 60%'): one clear offer, on a named product, at a real price.
short: No vague discounts ('40% or 60%'): one clear offer at a real price.
why: A muted viewer must understand the deal from one frame.

rule: No film, TV, football or music-video clips and no copyrighted songs: only the business's own photos and footage, generated shots and the BuPulse music library.
short: No film, TV, football clips or copyrighted songs.
why: The For You feed is full of borrowed clips (football, films); an ad account gets them muted or taken down.

rule: No two-minute scrolling lists in an ad: at most about 5 items, one per beat, or one price card that stays up.
why: A 136 s word list kept likes low (2.3K); price lists that work fit in one frame.

rule: 'Start your business with us' only for real wholesalers, and never with an income promise ('make $10k', 'say goodbye to poverty').
short: 'Start your business with us' only for real wholesalers, never with income promises.
why: Business-idea clips sell hope; a client ad must sell stock at a price.

rule: Do not copy the polished brand-film look of hotels and big brands (no price, no number) for a small seller: their ads can afford to skip the contact, a small business cannot.
short: No polished brand film without a price and number for a small seller.
why: ONOMO, Piramie and Dilara have budgets and no number in the video; every small Rwandan seller shows the number.
